lsj_entry_text: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο, gen. τούτου, ταύτης, τούτου, etc.: the dual fem. never in Att. , v. ὁ, ἡ, τό, init.:—demonstr. Pron., this, common from Hom. downwds. ORIGIN and FORMS: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο prob. arose from a reduplication of the demonstr. ὁ, ἡ , τό with insertion of -υ- (= Skt. Particle u), e.g. ταῦτα fr. τα-υ-τα: Dor. gen. sg. fem. τούτας Philol. 11 ; nom. pl. τοῦτοι, ταῦται A.D. Synt. 111.23 : the former occurs Sophr. 24 , GDI 3045 B 6 (Selinus), SIG 339.16 (Rhodes, iii B. C.), etc., the latter is dub. in Sophr. 97 , certain in SIG 241 B 117 (Delph., iv B. C.): in Boeot. all forms begin with οὑτ-, as gen. sg. neut. οὕτω Supp.Epigr. 3.359.11 (iii B. C.); acc. sg. fem. οὕταν Corinn. Supp. 2.80 ; acc. pl. neut. οὗτα SIG 1185.20 (Tanagra, iii B. C.), etc.: gen. pl. fem. Att. τούτων, Cret. ταυτᾶν Leg.Gort. 5.19 ; neut. ταύτων Michel 1334.10 (Elis, iv B. C.).—In Ion. sts. written ταότην, ταο ͂τα, SIG 283.19 (Chios, iv B. C.), 46.7 (Halic., v B. C.), al.—In Att. οὗτος was freq. strengthd. by the demonstr. -ί, οὑτοσί, αὑτηί, τουτί, gen. τουτουί, dat. τουτῳί, acc. τουτονί; pl. nom. οὑτοιί, neut. ταυτί, etc., this man here: sts. a Particle is inserted between the Pron. and -ί, as αὑτηγί for αὑτηί γε, Ar. Ach. 784 ; τουτογί for τουτί γε, Id. V. 781 , Av. 894 , al.; ταυταγί for ταυτί γε, Id. Eq. 492 , Pax 1057 , al.; τουτοδί for τουτὶ δέ, Id. Pl. 227 ; τουτουμενί for τουτουὶ μέν, Id. Ra. 965 .—In codd. the ν ἐφελκυστικόν is sts. added in the forms οὑτοσίν, οὑτωσίν, and οὑτοσίν is said to be Att. by A.D. Pron. 59.24 , 82.11 . [This ι is always long, and a long vowel or diphthong before it becomes short, as αὑτηί, τουτῳί, οὑτοιί, Ar. Nu. 201 , Pl. 44 , Ach. 40 , etc.] USAGE in regard to CONCOR D. οὗτος is freq. used as a Pron. Subst.: hence neut. is folld. by gen., κατὰ τοῦτο τῆς ἀκροπόλιος Hdt. 1.84 ; εἰς τοῦθ' ὕβρεως ἐλήλυθεν D. 4.37 ; εἰς τοῦθ' ἥκεις μανίας Id. 36.48 ; ταῦτα τῶν μαθημάτων Pl. Euthd. 278b : but quite as freq. as Adj., in which case its Subst. commonly takes the Art., οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ or ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος.—But the Art. is absent, always in Ep. Poets (exc. Od. 18.114 ), οὗτος ἀνήρ Il. 14.471 , Od. 1.406 , etc.: sts. also in Trag., A. Pers. 122 (lyr.), 495 , S. Ph. 406 , OC 471 , 1177 : once in an Inscr., τοπεῖα: τούτων τὰ ἡμίσεα τοπείων IG 22.1622.135 (iv B. C.). sts. when the Noun is so specified that the Art. is not needed, ἐς γῆν ταύτην . . , ἥντινα νῦν Σκύθαι νέμονται Hdt. 4.8 ; ταύτας ἃς οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν μελέτας Th. 1.85 , cf. Pl. R. 449d , etc.; πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος, ὃν θρηνεῖς ἀεί S. El. 530 . when οὗτος is used in local sense, here, v. infr. c. 1.5 . when the Noun with which οὗτος agrees stands as its Predicate, αὕτη γὰρ ἦν σοι πρόφασις S. Ph. 1034 ; δικαστοῦ αὕτη ἀρετή [ἐστι] Pl. Ap. 18a : this exception extends to cases in which the Predicate is not so distinctly separated from the Subject, αἰτίαι μὲν αὗται προυγεγένηντο these were the grievances which already existed, Th. 1.66 ; ταύτην φήμην παρέδοσαν this was the report which . . , Pl. Phlb. 16c : freq. with a Sup. , κίνησις αὕτη μεγίστη δὴ . . ἐγένετο this was notably the greatest movement which . . , Th. 1.1 , cf. 3.113 : with πρῶτος Id. 1.55 , 98 , 6.31 , Ev.Luc. 2.2 . when 3rd pers. is used for 2nd to express contempt, οὗτος ἀνήρ, οὑτοσὶ ἀνήρ, Pl. Grg. 467b , 489b , etc. though οὗτος usu. agrees with the Noun that serves as Predicate, it is not rare to find it in the neut., μανία δὲ καὶ τοῦτ' ἐστί E. Ba. 305 ; τοῦτο γάρ εἰσι . . εὔθυναι D. 19.82 , etc.: and in pl., οὐκ ἔστι ταῦτα ἀρχή Aeschin. 3.13 ; ταῦτ' ἐστὶν ὁ προδότης Id. 2.166 : so with an explanatory clause added, τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ὁ συκοφάντης, αἰτιᾶσθαι μὲν πάντα ἐξελέγξαι δὲ μηδέν D. 57.34 . so also with a Noun in apposition, τούτοισιν μὲν ταῦτα μέλει, κίθαρις καὶ ἀοιδή Od. 1.159 ; τούτου τιμῶμαι, ἐν πρυτανείῳ σιτήσεως Pl. Ap. 36e , cf. E. Fr. 323.3 , etc. the neut. also may refer to a masc. or fem. Noun, καρπὸν φορέει κυάμῳ ἴσον: τοῦτο ἐπεὰν γένηται πέπον κτλ. Hdt. 4.23 , cf. X. An. 1.5.10 , etc. the neut. is also used of classes of persons, μελιτοπῶλαι καὶ τυροπῶλαι: τοῦτο δ' εἰς ἕν ἐστι συγκεκυφός Ar. Eq. 854 , cf. Pl. Lg. 711a ; or of an abstract fact, οὐκ Ἰοφῶν ζῇ;—τοῦτο γάρ τοι καὶ μόνον ἔτ' ἐστὶ λοιπὸν ἀγαθόν Ar. Ra. 73 . with Prons., personal, οὗτος σύ, in local sense, v. infr. c. 1.5 . interrog., τί τοῦτ' ἔλεξας; what is this that . . ? S. Ph. 1173 (lyr.), cf. Ant. 7 ; ποίοισι τούτοις; for ποῖά ἐστι ταῦτα οἷς [ἔχεις ἐλπίδα]; Id. OC 388 , cf. Ant. 1049 ; Νέστορ' ἔρειο ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγει whom he brings here, Il. 11.612 . with οἷος, Od. 20.377 , Pl. Phd. 61c . possess., πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος this father of thine, S. El. 530 , cf. X. An. 7.3.30 . demonstr., οὗτος ἐκεῖνος, τὸν σὺ ζητέεις, where ἐκεῖνος is the Predicate, Hdt. 1.32 ; τοῦτ' ἔστ' ἐκεῖνο E. Hel. 622 , cf. Or. 804 ; αὐτὸ τοῦτο, v. αὐτός 1.7; τοῦτον τὸν αὐτὸν ἄνδρα this same man, S. Ph. 128 . exceptionally, Διφίλου οὗτος ὅδ' ἐστὶ τύπος IG 12(5).300 (Paros). ἄλλος τις οὗτος ἀνέστη another man here, Od. 20.380 . with Numerals, τέθνηκε ταῦτα τρία ἔτη these three years, Lys. 7.10c odd.; [στρατείαν] ἑνδέκατον μῆνα τουτονὶ ποιεῖται for these eleven months, D. 8.2 , cf. 3.4 ; τριακοστὴν ταύτην ἡμέραν Men. Epit. 27 ; ταύτας τριάκοντα μνᾶς D. 27.23 , cf. Pl. Grg. 463b , etc. SIGNIFICATION AND SPECIAL IDIOMS: this, to designate the nearer, opp. ἐκεῖνος, that, the more remote, ταῦτα, like τὰ ἐνταῦθα , things round and about us, earthly things, Pl. Phd. 75e (v. l.); cf. ὅδε init.: but οὗτος sts. indicates that which is not really nearest, but most important, δεῖ . . τὸ βέλτιστον ἀεί, μὴ τὸ ῥᾷστον λέγειν: ἐπὶ ἐκεῖνο μὲν γὰρ ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ βαδιεῖται, ἐπὶ τοῦτο δὲ κτλ. D. 8.72 , cf. 51.3 and 18 . when, of two things, one precedes and the other follows, ὅδε prop. refers to what follows, οὗτος to what precedes, οὐκ ἔστι σοι ταῦτ', ἀλλά σοι τάδ' ἔστι S. OC 787 , cf. ὅδε III. 2 : freq., however, where there are not two things, οὗτος refers to what follows, Il. 13.377 , Od. 2.306 , etc.; οὔκουν . . τοῦτο γιγνώσκεις, ὅτι . . ; A. Pr. 379 , etc. οὗτος is used emphat., generally in contempt, while ἐκεῖνος denotes praise, ὁ πάντ' ἄναλκις οὗτος, i.e. Aegisthus, S. El. 301 ; τούτους τοὺς συκοφάντας Pl. Cri. 45a ; so D. de Coron. uses οὗτος of Aeschines, ἐκεῖνος of Philip; but οὗτος is used of Philip, D. 2.15 , 4.3 . of what is familiar, τούτους τοὺς πολυτελεῖς χιτῶνας, of the Persians, X. An. 1.5.8 ; οἱ τὰς τελετὰς . . οὗτοι καταστήσαντες Pl. Phd. 69c , cf. Men. 80a ; τὸ θυλακῶδες τοῦτο the familiar bag-like thing, Thphr. HP 3.7.3 , cf. 3.18.11 , 4.7.1 ; οἱ τὰς κόρας ταύτας ὠνούμενοι τοῖς παισίν D.Chr. 31.153 . in Att. law-language, οὗτος is commonly applied to the opponent, whether plaintiff (as in Aeschin. 2.130 ) or defendant (as in Id. 1.1 ); so, in the political speeches of D. , οὗτοι are the opposite party, 4.1 , 8.7 , etc.; but in the forensic speeches, οὗτοι freq. means the judges, the court, 21.134 , 36.47 . much like an Adv., in local sense (cf. ὅδε init.), τίς δ' οὗτος κατὰ νῆας . . ἔρχεαι; who art thou here that comest . . ? Il. 10.82 ; freq. in Att. , τίς οὑτοσί; who's this here? Ar. Ach. 1048 ; πολλὰ ὁρῶ ταῦτα πρόβατα I see many sheep here, X. An. 3.5.9 (as v.l.): with Pron. of 2 pers., οὗτος σύ ho you! you there! S. OT 532 , 1121 , E. Hec. 1280 , etc.: and then οὗτος alone like a voc., οὗτος, τί ποιεῖς; A. Supp. 911 ,cf. S. Aj. 71 , E. Alc. 773 , Ar. Eq. 240 , Nu. 220 , al.: with a pr. n., ὦ οὗτος, Αἴας S. Aj. 89 ; ὦ οὗτος οὗτος, Οἰδίπους Id. OC 1627 , cf. Ar. V. 1364 : with voc., βέντισθ' οὗτος Theoc. 5.76 :—the fem. is rarer, αὕτη E. Med. 922 ; αὕτη σύ Ar. Th. 610 .—This phrase mostly implies anger, impatience, or scorn. simply as antec. to ὅς, Od. 2.40 , S. OT 1180 , etc.: freq. following relat. clause, ἅ γ' ἔλαβες, . . μεθεῖναι ταῦτα Id. Ph. 1247 , cf. 1319 , Ant. 183 , 203 , Pl. Grg. 469c . = τοιοῦτος, οὗτος ἐγὼ ταχυτᾶτι Pi. O. 4.26 ; σὺ τοίνυν οὗτος εὑρέθης D. 18.282 , cf. 173 . after a parenthesis, the Subject, though already named, is freq. emphat. repeated by οὗτος, οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ Ἀριστέης . . , οὐδὲ οὗτος προσωτέρω . . ἔφησε ἀπικέσθαι Hdt. 4.16 , cf. 81 (s. v. l.), 1.146 , Pl. Phd. 107d , etc. καὶ οὗτος is added to heighten the force of a previous word, ξυνεστῶτες . . ναυτικῷ ἀγῶνι, καὶ τούτῳ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους Th. 4.55 , cf. Hdt. 1.147 , 6.11 , etc.; so οὐδὲ τούτου Aeschin. 2.100 ; v. infr. VIII. 2 . repeated, where for the second we should merely say he or it, τοῖσιν τούτου τοῦτον μέλεσιν . . κελαδοῦντες Ar. Ra. 1526 , cf. Pl. La. 200d . ταῦτα is used in some special phrases, ταῦτ', ὦ δέσποτα yes Sir (i. e. ἔστι ταῦτα, ταῦτα δράσω, etc.), Ar. V. 142 , Pax 275 , cf. Eq.III; so ταῦτα δή Id. Ach. 815 ; ταῦτά νυν Id. V. 1008 ; so also ἦν ταῦτα even so, true, E. Ph. 417 . ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ὑπάρξει so it shall be, Pl. Phd. 78a . καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα so much for that, freq. in Att. , as Pl. Smp. 220c . ταῦτα at end of a formula in epitaphs, etc., prob. short for ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει or ὁ βίος ταῦτά ἐστιν, e.g. οὐδὶς ( = -εὶς ) ἀθάνατος: ταῦτα IG 14.420 ; Προκόπι ταῦτα ib. 1824 ; χαίρεται ( = -τε ) ταῦτα ib. 1479 , etc.: similarly perh. in a letter, ἂμ μὴ πέμψῃς, οὐ μὴ φάγω, οὐ μὴ πείνω. ταῦτα POxy. 119.15 (ii/iii A. D.). Adverbial usages: ταῦταabs., therefore, that is why . . , Il. 11.694 ; ταῦτ' ἄρα Ar. Ach. 90 , Nu. 319 , 335 , 394 , al., X. Smp. 4.55 ; ταῦτα δή A. Pers. 159 , Pl. Smp. 174a ; ταῦτ' οὖν S. Tr. 550 , Ar. V. 1358 , etc.; αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἥκω, ἵνα . . Pl. Prt. 310e : τοῦτο is rare in this sense, τοῦτ' ἀφικόμην, ὅπως . . εὖ πράξαιμί τι S. OT 1005 ; αὐτὸ γὰρ τοῦτο just because of this, Pl. Smp. 204a . πρὸς ταῦτα so then, therefore, prop. used in indignant defiance, A. Pr. 992 , 1043 , S. Aj. 971 , 1115 , 1313 , OT 426 , OC 455 , etc. καὶ ταῦτα, adding a circumstance heightening the force of what has been said, and that, ἄνδρα γενναῖον θανεῖν, καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς γυναικός A. Eu. 627 : but mostly with a part., ὅς γ' ἐξέλυσας ἄστυ . . , καὶ ταῦθ' ὑφ' ἡμῶν οὐδὲν ἐξειδὼς πλέον S. OT 37 , cf. Ar. Ra. 704 , Pl. Phdr. 241e , etc.; or with a part. omitted, ἥτις . . τὴν τεκοῦσαν ὕβρισεν, καὶ ταῦτα τηλικοῦτος (sc. οὖσα) S. El. 614 ; so καὶ ταῦτα μέντοι Pl. Erx. 400b . καὶ ταῦτα anyhow, no matter what happens (or happened), ἐπεχείρησας, οὐδὲν ὢν καὶ ταῦτα you tried, but were no good anyhow, i.e. try as you might, Id. R. 341c , cf. Diod.Com. 3.5 . τοῦτο μέν . . , τοῦτο δέ . . on the one hand . . , on the other . . , partly . . , partly . . , very freq. in Hdt. , as 1.161 , al.; τοῦτο μέν is sts. answered by δέ only, 4.76 , S. Aj. 670 , OC 440 ; by δὲ αὖ, Hdt. 7.176 ; by ἔπειτα δέ, S. Ant. 61 ; by ἀλλά, D. 22.13 ; by εἶτα, S. Ph. 1345 ; by τοῦτ' αὖθις, Id. Ant. 165 . dat. fem. ταύτῃ, on this spot, here, ταύτῃ μὲν . . , τῇδε δ' αὖ . . Id. Ph. 1331 ; ἀλλ' ἐὰν ταύτῃ γε νικᾷ, ταυτῃὶ πεπλήξεται Ar. Eq. 271 , cf. Th. 1221 . in this point, herein, μηδὲν ταύτῃ γε κομήσῃς Id. Pl. 572 , cf. X. Hier. 7.12 , etc. in this way, thus, A. Pr. 191 , S. OC 1300 , etc.; οὐ . . ταῦτ' ἐστί πω ταύτῃ Ar. Eq. 843 ; ἀλλ' οὔτι ταύτῃ ταῦτα E. Med. 365 , cf. A. Pr. 511 : antec. to ὥσπερ, Pl. R. 330c ; to ὅπῃ, X. Cyr. 8.3.2 ; οὕτω τε καὶ ταύτῃ γίγνοιτο Pl. Lg. 681d ; καὶ οὕτω καὶ ταύτῃ ἂν ἔχοι ib. 714d ; ταύτῃ καλεῖσθαι, etc., like οὕτω κ. , Sch. Pl. Smp. 215b . ἐκ τούτου or τούτων thereupon, X. HG 3.1.6 , Oec. 2.1 ; therefore, Id. An. 3.3.5 . ἐν τούτῳ in that case, Pl. R. 440c . in the meantime, Hdt. 1.126 , Th. 3.72 , X. Mem. 2.1.27 . πρὸς τούτοις (-οισι) besides, Hdt. 2.51 , Pl. Prt. 326a , X. Mem. 2.4.4 , Ar. Pl. 540 .

lsj_entry_text: φάρμακον [v. sub fin.], τό, drug, whether healing or noxious: in Hom. the sense is freq. determined by an epith., φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ . . , πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά Od. 4.230 ; τόδε φ. ἐσθλόν 10.287 , cf. 292 ; φ. ἤπια, ὀδυνήφατα (v. infr. 2 ); κακὰ φ. ib. 213 ; φ. λυγρά ib. 236 ; φ. οὐλόμενον ib. 394 ; ἀνδροφόνον 1.261 ; θυμοφθόρα φ. 2.329 ; so, after Hom. , προσανέα φ. greek_sentence: Περὶ κόπρου τῶν χερσαίων κροκοδείλων καὶ ψάρων.] Τὴν δὲ τῶν χερσαίων κροκοδείλων τούτων τῶν μικρῶν τε καὶ χαμαιρεπῶν κόπρον ἔντιμον αἱ τρυφῶσαι πεποιήκασι γυναῖκες, αἷς οὐκ ἀρκέσει τοῖς ἄλλοις φαρμάκοις τοσούτοις οὖσιν λαμπρόν τε καὶ τετανὸν ἐργάσασθαι τὸ περὶ τὸ πρόσωπον δέρμα, προστιθέασι δ’ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὴν τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρον.
english_sentence_A: On the dung of land crocodiles and of starlings.] The dung of these land crocodiles, the small ones that creep along the ground, luxurious women have made a thing of high esteem, women for whom it will not suffice to render the skin about the face bright and taut with the other drugs, numerous as they are, but they add to these also the dung of crocodiles.
english_sentence_B: On the dung of land crocodiles and of starlings.] The dung of land crocodiles, those small ones that creep low along the ground, has been made a thing of value by luxury-loving women. It will not suffice them to make the skin of the face bright and taut with the other drugs, numerous as these are, but they add to them the crocodiles' dung as well.

english_sentence_B: Similar to it is also the dung of starlings, when they eat rice alone.

english_sentence_A: And what is eaten of animals is chiefly the flesh; for indeed the greater bulk of the viscera too is made up of the flesh in them.

lsj_entry_text: μαλακ-τικός, ή, όν, emollient, χρίσματα Hp. Vict. 2.66 ; δύναμις Plu. 2.659c ; μ. οἶκος, of the outer chamber in a bath, Alex. Trall. Febr. 5 .
greek_sentence: Περὶ μυελοῦ.] Μυελὸς μαλακτικῆς τῶν σκληρυνομένων τε καὶ σκιῤῥουμένων σωμάτων ἐστὶ δυνάμεως, εἴτε μύες εἴτε τένοντες εἴτε σύνδεσμοι τοῦτο πάσχοιεν εἴτε καὶ σπλάγχνα.
english_sentence_A: On marrow.] Marrow is of a softening power for bodies that are becoming hardened and scirrhous, whether it be muscles, tendons or ligaments that suffer this, or even viscera.
english_sentence_B: On marrow.] Marrow is of a power softening of bodies that are hardened and becoming scirrhous, whether muscles or tendons or ligaments suffer this, or also viscera.

(-φος as in ἔρι-φος, etc., ἐλα- from ἐλ ṇ-, cf. ἐλλός (from Ἐλνός), Lith. élnis 'stag'.)
greek_sentence: καλλίστου δ’ ἐπειράθην ἀεὶ τοῦ τῶν ἐλάφων, ἐφεξῆς δ’ αὐτῶν τοῦ τῶν νέων βοῶν, οὓς δὴ καὶ μόσχους καλοῦσι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὸν μυελὸν αὐτῶν ὀνομάζουσι μόσχειον.
english_sentence_A: I have always found that of deer the best, and next after it that of young cattle, which indeed they also call calves (moschoi), and for this reason they also name their marrow 'calf-marrow' (moscheion).
english_sentence_B: I have always found by experience that the marrow of deer is the best, and next after it that of young cattle, whom they also call calves (moschoi), and for this reason they name their marrow too 'calf's marrow' (moscheios).

english_sentence_A: From calf and deer marrow, then, softening pessaries are compounded for the affections of the womb, and medicines prepared with marrow, having a softening power, are applied externally over the womb itself.
english_sentence_B: From calf's and deer's marrow, at any rate, softening pessaries are compounded for conditions in the uterus, and drugs prepared with marrow, having a softening power, are applied over the uterus itself from outside.

lsj_entry_text: ὑγρός, ά, όν: Comp. ὑγρότερος Pl. Tht. 162b , etc.: Sup. -ότατος X. Eq. 7.7 , etc.:—wet, moist, fluid (opp. ξηρός), ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον, i. e. olive-oil, opp. fat or tallow, Il. 23.281 , Od. 6.79 ; ὑ. πίσσα, νᾶπυ, raw pitch, liquid mustard, SIG 1171.14 (Lebena, i B. C.), IG 42(1).126.22 (Epid., ii A. D.); τὸ ὑ. ξύλον, opp. τὸ ξηρόν, Ev.Luc. 23.31 ; ὑγρὸν ὕδωρ Od. 4.458 ; ἄνεμοι ὑγρὸν ἀέντες winds blowing moist or rainy, 5.478 , 19.440 , Hes. Op. 625 , Th. 869 ; ὑ. ἅλς, πέλαγος, θάλασσα, Pi. O. 7.69 . P. 4.40 , A. Supp. 259 ; ὑγρὰ νύξ a wet night, Pl. Criti. 112a ; ἐφ' ὑγροῖς ζωγραφεῖν paint on a wet ground, Plu. 2.759c . ὑγρά, Ion. ὑγρή, ἡ, the moist, i.e. the sea, ἐπὶ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν Il. 14.308 ; ἠμὲν ἐφ' ὑγρὴν ἠδ' ἐπ' ἀπείρονα γαῖαν 24.341 , Od. 1.97 ; ἐφ' ὑγρᾷ Ar. V. 678 ; πουλὺν ἐφ' ὑγρήν Il. 10.27 ; so ὑγρὰ κέλευθα the watery ways, i. e. the sea, 1.312 , Od. 3.71 . τὸ ὑ. and τὰ ὑ. wet, moisture, Hdt. 1.142 , Hp. Loc.Hom. 9 , Liqu. tit.; Liquid, Hdt. 4.172 ; γῆ ὑγρῷ φυραθεῖσα Pl. Tht. 147c ; ἐξερρύα συχνὸν ὑγρόν a quantity of fluid, IG 42(1).122.4 (Epid., iv B. C.); μετρεῖν τὰ ὑγρά liquids, ib. 22.1013.10 ; ἐπὶ ὑγροῖς οὐκ ἐξὸν δανείζειν PGnom. 232 (ii A. D.). μέτρα ὑγρὰ καὶ ξηρά liquid and dry measure, Pl. Lg. 746e . θῆρες ὑ. water-animals, opp. πεζοί, AP 9.18 ( Germ. ); οἱ ὄρνιθες οἱ ὑ. Philostr. Im. 1.9 ; ὑ. ἀοιδός, of a frog, AP 6.43 (Plato). of the bowels or faeces, loose, Hp. Aph. 2.20 , Arist. HA 617a1 . ὑ. σφυγμός a damp pulse, defined by Gal. 19.405 . soft, pliant, supple, of the eagle's back, Pi. P. 1.9 ; of the limbs and body, ὑγραῖς ἐν ἀγκάλαις E. Fr. 941 , cf. Babr. 34.7 ; ὑγρὸς τὸ εἶδος, of Ἔρως, Pl. Smp. 196a ; νεώτερος καὶ ὑγρότερος, opp. σκληρός, Id. Tht. 162b ; χορῷ . . ἔτερπον κέαρ ὑγροῖσι ποσσί B. 16.108 ; ὑ. ὀρχηστής Poll. 4.96 , cf. Arist. PA 655a24 ( Comp. ); ὑγρὰ ἔχειν τὰ σκέλη, of a horse, X. Eq. 1.6 ; of a horse's neck, Id. Cyn. 4.1 (so in Adv. of colts, γόνατα ὑγρῶς κάμπτειν, ὑγρῶς τοῖς σκέλεσι χρῆσθαι, Id. Eq. 1.6 , 10.15 ); of the hare, Id. Cyn. 5.31 ; of the jackal, ταχυτῆτι διαφέρει διὰ τὸ ὑγρὸς εἶναι καὶ πηδᾷ πόρρω Arist. HA 580a30 ; also of plants, ὑ. ἄκανθος Theoc. 1.55 ; ὑ. χολάδες Babr. 1.10 ; σῶμα ὑγρὸν κείμενον lying in an easy position, Hp. Prog. 3 ; ὑγρὸν χύτλασον σεαυτόν Ar. V. 1213 ; κέρας ὑ., of a bow, Theoc. 25.206 . languid, feeble, of one dying, ἐς ὑγρὸν ἀγκῶνα . . παρθένῳ προσπτύσσεται S. Ant. 1236 ; κἀπιθεὶς ὑγρὰν χέρα E. Ph. 1439 . of substance, flaccid, flabby, σάρκες Arist. HA 598a9 , 603b32 , al. tender, νεοττοί Ael. NA 7.9 ; βρέφος Nonn. D. 1.4 . moist with wine, tipsy, ὑγρὴν τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχειν Heraclit. 117 ; ἡ διάνοια ὑ. γεγενημένη Plu. 2.713a ; οἰνοβαρὴς . . ὑγρὸν ἀείδων, οὐ μάλα νγφάλιον κλάζων μέλος Opp. H. 2.412 . of the eyes, melting, languishing, ὑ. βλέμμα Anacreont. 15.21 ; ὑγρὰ δερκομένοισιν ἐν ὄμμασιν AP 7.27 (Antip. Sid.); ἐπ' ὄμμασιν ὑγρὰ δεδορκώς APl. 4.306 ( Leon. ); τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν τὸ ὑ. ἅμα τῷ φαιδρῷ Luc. Im. 6 ; also πόθος ὑ. a languishing, longing desire, h.Pan. 33 . Adv., ὑγρῶς βλέπειν Philostr. Ep. 33 : Sup. , ὑγρότατα καὶ πένθιμα μελῳδεῖν App. BC 1.106 . of language, smoothly flowing, D.H. Dem. 20 . metaph. of persons or their tempers, facile, pliant, easy, ὑγρός τις καὶ δημοτικός Plu. Mar. 28 ; κόλαξ ὑγρὸς ὢν μεταβάλλεσθαι Id. 2.51c ; τὸ Κίμωνος ὑ. his easy temper, Id. Per. 5 ; pleasure-loving, Hsch. ; ὑγρότατος ἐς ταῦτα prone to . . , App. BC 5.8 ; ὑ. τῷ γελοίῳ Plu. Brut. 29 ( Comp. ). soft, dainty, luxurious, voluptuous, Id. 2.751a ; ὑ. πρὸς τὴν δίαιταν Id. english_sentence_A: But if ever, when the surrounding air is hot and humid, you should wish to store away marrows or fat, let a room be prepared for you that is neither hot—such as those facing south especially are, for in such rooms they rot—nor underground and damp, for in such rooms they grow mouldy, but one that is upstairs and facing north, with small windows thrown open so as to receive the northerly winds by day and by night.
english_sentence_B: And if ever you should wish to put away marrows or suet when the surrounding air is hot and humid, let a room be prepared for you that is neither hot, as are especially those facing south, for it rots in such rooms, nor underground and damp, for it grows mouldy in such rooms, but upper and facing north, having small windows open so as to receive the northern winds by day and by night.

greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐλάφου τινὲς τῶν γραψάντων τὰ τοιαῦτα μάλιστ’ ἐπαινοῦσιν, ὡς εἰ μετὰ τὸ καυθῆναι πλυθείη καὶ δυσεντερίαν καὶ πτύσιν ﻿ αἵματος, ἔτι τε τὰς καλουμένας κοιλιακὰς διαθέσεις ἐκθεραπεύειν, ἰκτερικοῖς τε διδόμενον ὠφέλιμον, ἐπὶ πάντων δὲ τούτων κελεύουσι διδόναι κοχλιάρια δύο, μεμίχασι δὲ αὐτό τινες, ὡς εἴρηται, κεκαυμένον τε καὶ πεπλυμένον καὶ τοῖς ξηραίνουσι κολλυρίοις τὰ ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς ῥεύματα.
english_sentence_A: Some of those who have written on such matters particularly commend that of the deer, claiming that, if after being burnt it is washed, it also thoroughly cures dysentery and spitting of blood, and further the so-called coeliac conditions, and that given to those suffering from jaundice it is beneficial; and in all these cases they prescribe giving two spoonfuls. Some have also mixed it, as has been said, burnt and washed, into the drying collyria for the fluxes in the eyes.
english_sentence_B: Some of those who have written on such matters especially praise that of the deer, [saying] that, if after being burnt it is washed, it thoroughly cures dysentery and spitting of blood, and furthermore the so-called coeliac conditions, and that when given to those with jaundice it is beneficial; and in all these cases they direct that two spoonfuls be given. Some have also mixed it, burnt and washed as has been said, into the collyria that dry up the fluxes in the eyes.

lsj_entry_text: ὄνυξ, υχος, ὁ, Hom. only in Ep. dat. pl. ὀνύχεσσι, and always of the eagle, talons, claws, Il. 8.248 , al. ; so of the falcon, Hes. Op. 204 , 205 , Ar. Av. 1180 ; so of beasts of prey, Pi. N. 4.63 , Hdt. 3.108 ; of the crocodile, Id. 2.68 ; of the Sphinx, E. El. 471 (lyr.); of human beings, nail, Hes. Sc. 266 , Hdt. 4.64 , etc.; τοὺς ὄνυχας τῶν δακτύλων Ar. Av. 8 ; of horses and oxen, hoof, X.Eq. 1.3 , Ap 9.64 ( Asclep. or Arch. ): Arist. speaks of the hoof (ὁπλή) as homologous to the nail or claw (ὄνυξ), HA 486b20 , PA 690a9 : metaph., πρὸς ὀξύν γ' ὄ. πετραίου λίθου E. Cyc. 401 codd. (leg. στόνυχα) :—Special phrases : εἰς ἄκρους τοὺς ὄ. ἀφίκετο (sc. ὁ οἶνος) warmed me to my fingers' ends, ib. 159 ; so ἐκ κορυφῆς εἰς ἄκρους ὄ. AP 9.709 ( Phil. ), cf. 12.93 ( Rhian. ) ; so also ἐξ ὀνύχων from the fingers' ends, ib. 5.13 ( Rufin. ), Plu. 2.3c ; but ἐξ ἁπαλῶν ὀ. from childhood, Horace's de tenero ungui, AP 5.128 ( Autom. ). ὄνυχας ἐπ' ἄκρους στάς on tiptoe, E. El. 840 ; ἐπ' ἄκρων ἐβάδιζε τῶν ὀ. Macho ap. Ath. 8.349b . ὅταν ἐν ὄνυχι ὁ πηλὸς γένηται, i. e. when the model reaches the nail stage, because the sculptor puts the finishing touches to the model with his nail, Polyclit. ap. Plu. 2.636c , cf. Dem. 13 ; σύμπηξις εἰς ὄνυχα a nice fit, Gal. 2.737 ; τὰς γωνίας ἐπ' ὄνυχος συμβεβλημένας ἔχειν Ph. Bel. 66.37 ; πρὸς ὄνυχα τὴν προσκαρτέρησιν ποιεῖσθαι Phld. (pl.), Paul.Aeg. 3.22.23 . part of the liver, Ruf. Onom. 180 , Sch. Nic. Th. 560 . veined gem, onyx, LXX Jb. 28.16 , Aristeas 66 , J. BJ 5.5.7 ; Σαρδῷος ὄ. sardonyx, Luc. english_sentence_A: Some say that the hooves of asses, when burnt, cure epileptics if they are drunk continuously, and that, kneaded with oil, they disperse scrofulous swellings; and that the same ash, sprinkled on dry, heals chilblains.
english_sentence_B: Some people say that the hooves of asses, burnt, cure epileptics if they are drunk continually, and that, kneaded with oil, they disperse choirades; and that the same ash, sprinkled on dry, heals chilblains (chimethla).

Op. 558 , Hdt. 1.203 ; τὰ λεπτὰ τῶν π. small cattle, i.e. sheep and goats, ib. 133 , 8.137 ; τὸ μὲν μέζον π. . . , τὸ δὲ μεῖον IG 5 ( 2 ). 3.14 (Tegea, iv B.C.); so later, π. ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρνῶν καὶ τῶν ἐρίφων λήψεσθε LXX Ex. 12.5 : but in Att. V. 32 : Com. english_sentence_A: On the skin of a sheep.] The skin of a sheep freshly flayed, wrapped around those who have been scourged in whatever manner, manifestly helps more than anything else, so as to cure them in a single day and night; for it both concocts and disperses the blood that has gathered under the skin.
english_sentence_B: On the skin of a sheep.] The skin of a sheep freshly flayed, wrapped around those who have been flogged in any way whatsoever, manifestly benefits them more than all other remedies, so as to heal them in one day and night; for it both concocts and disperses the blood-suffused parts.

greek_sentence: τῷ δ’ οὖν ὀστράκῳ τῶν ὀνομαζομένων ἰδίως ὀστρέων κεκαυμένῳ χρῶμαι πρὸς τὰς ἐκ ῥευμάτων χρονίας καὶ δυσσαρκώτους κοιλότητας, ὅσαι συραγγώδεις εἰσὶ καὶ βαθεῖαι, περιτεθεὶς ἔξωθεν αὐτὸ μετὰ παλαιοῦ στέατος ὑείου.
english_sentence_A: So I use the burnt shell of what are specifically called oysters for the chronic cavities arising from fluxes that are hard to fill with flesh, those that are fistulous and deep, applying it around on the outside together with old pig's fat.
english_sentence_B: I use the burnt shell of those that are properly called oysters for the chronic cavities that arise from fluxes and are hard to fill with flesh, those that are fistulous and deep, applying it on the outside with old pig's fat; this is called axungia by most people.

english_sentence_A: With salt, indeed, all such things when burnt make the dentifrice more effective, so as to dry flabby gums, but they also help putrid ulcers.

english_sentence_A: Now cleansing, as with the other shells of the shell-skinned animals, is common to it along with them, just as drying is too.

greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ τῆς οὐσίας λεπτομερὲς ἐξαίρετον αὐτῷ παρὰ τἄλλα ὑπάρχει, διὸ καὶ καυθέντι χρώμεθα πρὸς ἀλφοὺς ἔφηλίν τε καὶ φακοὺς καὶ ψώρας.
english_sentence_A: But the fine-particled quality of its substance belongs to it as something exceptional compared with the others, which is why we also use it, when burnt, for alphoi, ephelis, lentigines and scabies.
english_sentence_B: But the fine-particled nature of its substance belongs to it as a special property beyond the others; for this reason we also use it burnt for alphoi, ephelis, phakoi (lentil-spots) and psorai.

greek_sentence: ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ὀρυκτοῖς ἁλσὶ μιχθὲν ἀποτήκει τὰ κατ’ ὀφθαλμοὺς γινόμενα πτερύγια.
english_sentence_A: Moreover, mixed with mined salt it melts away the pterygia that form in the eyes.
english_sentence_B: Moreover, mixed with mined salt, it melts away the pterygia that arise on the eyes.

lsj_entry_text: σύμμετρ-ος, ον, (μέτρον) commensurate with, of like measure or size with, σύμμετρος σῷ ποδί (sc. ἡ βάσις) E. El. 533 ; χαμεύνῃ Id. Fr. 676 ; βόστρυχον . . σύμμετρον τῷ σῷ κάρᾳ exactly like it, A. Ch. 230 : esp. of Time, commensurate with, keeping even with, δαλὸν ἥλικα ξύμμετρόν τε διαὶ βίου ib. 610 (lyr.); τῷδε τἀνδρὶ ς. being of like age with him, S. OT 1113 ; ποίᾳ ξύμμετρος προὔβην τύχῃ; coincident with what chance have I come? i.e. in the very nick of time, Id. Ant. 387 , cf. E. Alc. 26 (infr. 111 ). in Mathematics, having a common measure, σύμμετροι αἱ τῷ αὐτῷ μέτρῳ μετρούμεναι (sc. γραμμαί) Arist. LI 968b6 ; freq. denied of the relation between the diagonal of a square and its side, Id. APo. 71b27 , APr. 41a26 , Ph. 221b25 , Rh. 1392a18 ; [τὸ νόμισμα] πάντα ποιεῖ σύμμετρα commensurable, Id. EN 1133b22 ; μήκει οὐ σύμμετροι τῇ ποδιαίᾳ not lineally commensurate with the one-foot side, Pl. Tht. 147d , cf. 148b : Comp. , of musical intervals, ταῖς αἰσθήσεσιν εὐληπτότερα τὰ -ότερα Ptol. Harm. 1.10 . in accord with the metre, S. Eleg. 1 ; σύμμετροι ἐπεκτύπεον ποδῶν χορείαις in time, Tim. Pers. 213 . in measure with, proportionable, exactly suitable, λόγοι ἀνδράσι ς. Isoc. 4.83 , cf. 5.110 , 12.135 ; γῆ θηρίοις μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις ς. Str. 15.1.26 ; ς. πρός τι Pl. Lg. 625d , Metrod. Fr. 1 , etc.; c. dat., Pl. Men. 76d , Ti. 67c , Epicur. Fr. 81 ( Comp. ). abs., in right measure, in due proportion, symmetrical, opp. ὑπερβάλλων and ἐλλείπων, Arist. EN 1104a18 , al.; τὸ ς. καὶ καλόν Pl. Phlb. 66b ; τῶν φύσει ξηροτέρων . . ὡς πρὸς τὸν ς. παραβάλλειν Gal. 6.360 , cf. 27 , al. generally, fitting, meet, due, ξύμμετρον δ' ἔπος λέγω A. Eu. 532 (lyr.); δένδρον πολυκαρπότερον τοῦ συμμέτρου Pl. Ti. 86c , cf. Phld. Rh. 1.288S. , al.; ξύμμετρος ὡς κλύειν within fit distance for hearing, S. OT 84 . moderate, πόνοι Isoc. 1.12 ; ὥστε σύμμετρον . . τὸ πνεῦμα . . ποιεῖν Antiph. 202.16 ; ς. τροφαί Sor. 1.26 , cf. 49 , al.; ς. στέγη moderate in size, X. Oec. 8.13 ; of suitable size, σκῆπτρον OGI 56.62 (Canopus, iii B.C.). Adv. -τρως in moderation, Isoc. 1.32 , etc.; in due time, ἀφίκετο E. Alc. 26 ; ς. πρὸς ἑωυτόν conveniently, Hp. Off. 3 ; ς. ἔχειν πρός τι to be in proportion to . ., X. Eq. 1.16 ; εἴς τι Arist. Mir. 834a15 ; ς. ἴσχειν λεπτότητος καὶ πάχους Pl. Ti. 85c ; τὸ μετὰ νοῦ καὶ τὸ ς. Nicom.Com. 1.36 ; = μετρίως, φέρειν IG 12(7).396.31 (Amorgos, ii B.C.), cf. Aristid.Quint. 2.5 . Comp. -ότερον more fittingly, D. 61.27 ( v.l. -ώτερον ).
greek_sentence: τῷ συμμέτρῳ αὐτοῦ τῆς τραχύτητος καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς μεγάλας τραχύτητας, ἃς καλοῦσιν συκώσεις, εἰώθαμεν χρῆσθαι, διαγλύφοντες ἐξ αὐτοῦ παραπλήσιόν τι κολλυρίῳ κατὰ τὸ σχῆμα καὶ ἀνατρίβοντες αὐτὰς ὡς αἱμάξαι.
english_sentence_A: On account of the moderate degree of its roughness we are also accustomed to use it for the great roughnesses in the eyes which they call sycoses, carving out of it something resembling a collyrium in shape and rubbing them with it so as to draw blood.
english_sentence_B: We are also accustomed to use the moderate degree of its roughness against the great roughnesses in the eyes which they call sykōseis: we carve out of it something resembling a collyrium in shape and rub them with it so as to draw blood.

lsj_entry_text: καθαιρ-ετικός, ή, όν, destructive, c. gen., Corn. ND 30 , Ph. 2.548 . reducing, catheretic, φάρμακα, of mild caustics, Gal. 11.756 ; σπληνὸς καθαιρετικόν Dsc. 2.112 ; putting a stop to, παλμῶν Gal. 7.600 : generally, ὑγίεια κ. παθῶν Ph. Fr. 103H.
greek_sentence: τούτου γὰρ γενομένου καὶ τὰ καθαιρετικὰ τῶν κολλυρίων ἄμεινον ἐπ’ αὐτῶν ἐνεργεῖ.
english_sentence_A: For when this has been done, the reducing collyria too act better upon them.
english_sentence_B: For when this has been done, the reducing collyria also act better upon them.

greek_sentence: Περὶ πωμάτων πορφυρῶν.] Πώματα πορφυρῶν δι’ ὄξους ποθέντα σπλῆνας οἰδαλέους ἔγραψάν τινες ἰᾶσθαι, θυμιώμενα δὲ τὰς πνιγομένας ὑστερικῶς ὠφελεῖν ἐκβάλλειν τε τὰ κατεχόμενα χόρια.
english_sentence_A: On the lids of purple-shells.] Some have written that the lids (opercula) of purple-shells (porphyrai), drunk with vinegar, cure swollen spleens, and that, used as a fumigation, they benefit women who are being suffocated hysterically and expel retained afterbirth (choria).
english_sentence_B: On the lids of purple-shells.] Some have written that the lids of purple-shells, drunk in vinegar, cure swollen spleens, and that, used as a fumigation, they benefit women who are suffocated hysterically, that is, from the womb, and expel retained afterbirths.

english_sentence_A: Now the white and thin part of eggs, which we also use for ophthalmias, is among the least biting of drugs, nor have I met with failure from such a dyskrasia as milk often has, as we showed earlier in the case of animals that have failed to digest or have been excessively hungry or excessively thirsty or have used bad foods, things which indeed tend to occur more in women on account of faultiness of regimen.
english_sentence_B: The white and thin part of eggs, which we also use for ophthalmias, is among the least biting of drugs, nor did they have any failure arising from such a dyscrasia as milk often has, as we showed earlier in the case of animals that have suffered indigestion, or have been excessively hungry or excessively thirsty, or have used bad foods, things which indeed tend to happen more in women because of error in regimen.

greek_sentence: ἐπιτηδειότεραι δ’ εἰσὶ πρὸς ἅπερ ἔφην λέγων πεπειράσθαι τῶν κανθαρίδων ἐκ τῶν πυρῶν ὅσαι μηλίνας ἐγκαρσίας ζώνας ἔχουσιν ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, καὶ μᾶλλον, ἐὰν ἐμβαλὼν αὐτὰς εἰς ἀγγεῖον καινὸν κεράμιον, εἶτα περιτιθεὶς τῷ στόματι τοῦ ἀγγείου τῶν ἀραιῶν ὀθονίων τι κρατῇς οὕτω τὸ ἀγγεῖον, ὡς ἐστράφθαι τὴν ὀθόνην κάτω, δεχομένην τὸν ἀναφερόμενον ἀτμὸν τοῦ ὄξους ἄχρις ἂν ἀποθάνωσιν αἱ κανθαρίδες.
english_sentence_A: The more suitable among the cantharides, for the purposes for which I said I had made trial of them, are those from the wheat which have quince-yellow transverse bands on their wings, and more so if, having put them into a new earthenware vessel and then fastened one of the loose-woven linen cloths around the mouth of the vessel, you hold the vessel in such a way that the linen is turned downward, receiving the vapour of the vinegar rising up, until the cantharides die.
english_sentence_B: More suitable for the purposes for which I said I had tested cantharides are those from the wheat that have transverse yellow bands on their wings; and they are more so if you put them into a new earthenware vessel, then place some piece of loose-woven linen over the mouth of the vessel, and hold the vessel in such a way that the linen is turned downwards, receiving the vapour of the vinegar that rises up, until the cantharides die.

english_sentence_A: So, having conceived the idea of applying it, while still alive, to someone suffering pain in the head—for it could be a pain-stilling drug, like the other things that numb sensation—I found that this is so.

english_sentence_A: On the sea-dragon and the red mullet.] They have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, bring benefit: the sea-dragon placed upon its own wound, and likewise also the red mullet upon that of the dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, just as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as curing its own bite.
english_sentence_B: On the sea dragon and the red mullet.] Some have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, are beneficial: the sea dragon placed upon its own sting, and likewise the red mullet upon that of the sea dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own bite, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as healing its own bite.

english_sentence_A: They say too that in the regions of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is employed with benefit for a dog's bite when placed upon the wound, and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length among the agents that act by the specific property of their whole substance.
english_sentence_B: They say also that in the districts of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is usefully employed for the bite of a dog, applied over the wound; and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length in the discussion of things that act by a peculiarity of the whole substance.

english_sentence_A: It has been said many times that it belongs to such drugs to draw toward the surface what is contained in the depth of the body, and for this reason sometimes to put a stop to pains.
english_sentence_B: It has been said many times that drugs of this kind have the property of drawing to the surface what is contained in the depth of the body, and in this way sometimes of stopping pains. For this does not follow from them in every case.

greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ δὴ διὰ παντός γε τοῦτ’ αὐτοῖς ἕπεται μόνον, ἐκείνων τῶν ὀδυνῶν παυομένων ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων φαρμάκων, ἐφ’ ὧν ἐν τῷ βάθει περιέχεται χυμὸς ὀδύνης ποιητικὸς, ἢ διὰ τὸ πάχος τῆς οὐσίας ἢ διὰ ψύξιν ἢ δριμύτητα σφοδρὰν ἢ καὶ πνεῦμα φυσῶδες, οὐκ ἔχον διέξοδον.
english_sentence_A: For it is certainly not in every case that this alone follows for them; those pains are stopped by such drugs in which a pain-producing humour is contained in the depth, either because of the thickness of its substance, or because of coldness or violent pungency, or even flatulent pneuma that has no way out.
english_sentence_B: Only those pains are stopped by such drugs in which a humour productive of pain is contained in the depth, whether because of the thickness of its substance, or because of coldness or violent pungency, or else a flatulent pneuma that has no outlet. Those, then, who used the foxes likewise made the oil dispersing.

english_sentence_A: Those, then, who used the foxes themselves also made the oil dispersing; then, filling tubs with it, they set the arthritics whole into them, bidding them remain in them for a considerable time, and from this it came about that not only the swellings around their joints but also the whole body was emptied.
english_sentence_B: Then, filling tubs with it, they set the arthritics in them whole, bidding them remain in them for a long time. From this it came about that not only the swellings about their joints but also the whole body was evacuated.

english_sentence_A: On adarkion.] Adarkion—some people call it, in the masculine, adarkos, others, in the feminine, adarke—is in its substance like a kind of congealed foam, formed by salty water congealing around rubbish and reeds.

english_sentence_A: On alkyonia.] Alkyonia all cleanse and disperse, having a pungent quality and a hot power, but the more and the less among them is not slight, both in these very respects which I have mentioned and moreover in respect of the fine-particled character of the whole substance.
english_sentence_B: On alkyonia.] All alkyonia are cleansing and dispersing, having a pungent quality and a hot power. But the more and the less among them is not slight, both in the very respects I have mentioned and, further, in how fine-particled their whole substance is.

Ra. 1387 ; οὖλα ἔρια ib. 1067 ; ἔ. πεπταμένα outspread flocks of wool, Id. Nu. 343 ; ἐρίων τάλαντον Id. V. 1147 ; τὰ Μιλήσια ἔ. Eub. 90.3 , cf. Amphis 27.1 ; εἴρια ἀπὸ ξύλου cotton, Hdt. 3 . 47 , cf. 106 ; τὸ ἔ. [τῆς ἀράχνησ] a spider's web, Philostr. Im. 2.28 ; τὰ ἐκ τῆς θαλάττης ἔ., of the byssus of the pinna, Alciphr. 1.2 . ( ἔρια Schwyzer 180 (Crete) without initial v-; Lat. vervex perh. not cogn.)
greek_sentence: ἐφ’ οἷς ἄλλο τέταρτον, ὁμοίως μὲν τῷ δευτέρῳ λελεγμένῳ κοῦφόν τε καὶ ἀραιὸν, ἐοικὸς δὲ ἐρίοις οἰσυπηροῖς.
english_sentence_A: In addition to these there is another, a fourth, light and loose-textured like the one mentioned second, but resembling greasy, unwashed wool.
english_sentence_B: Besides these there is a fourth, which is light and porous like the second one mentioned, but resembles greasy unwashed wool.

lsj_entry_text: λεία (B), Ion. ληΐη, Dor. λᾴα ( Pi. O. 10(11).44 ), ἡ, booty, plunder, freq. in Hdt. (v. infr.), etc. ( Hom. and Hes. always use ληΐς); esp. of cattle, opp. ἄνθρωποι, Pi.l.c., Th. 2.94 (v. infr. 4 ); λείας ἀπαρχὴν βοῦς S. Tr. 761 , cf. Aj. 54 , 145 (anap.): pl., ἐφθαρμένας εὑρίσκομεν λείας ἁπάσας ib. 26 ; rarely of persons, ἀγόμεθα λεία E. Tr. 614 ; prey of hunters, Id. Rh. 326 : generally, booty, Th. 8.3 , X. HG 1.2.4 , 1.3.2 ; τοὺς λοιποὺς ληΐην θέσθαι give them up as plunder, Hdt. 4.202 ; λείαν ποιεῖσθαι τὴν χώραν, = λεηλατεῖν τὴν χώραν , Th. 8.41 ; λείαν ἄγειν X. Cyr. 5.3.1 ; ἐπὶ λείαν ἐκπορεύσονται Id. An. 5.1.8 , etc.; κατὰ ληΐην ἐκπλῶσαι Hdt. 2.152 : pl., διεσκεδασμένοι κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας λείας X. HG 1.2.5 : prov., Μυσῶν λεία, of anything that may be plundered with impunity, Stratt. 35 , D. 18.72 , Arist. Rh. 1372b33 . plunder (as an act), ζῶσι ἀπὸ ληΐης καὶ πολέμου Hdt. 4.103 . stolen property, τὴν λ. ἀποδοῦναι PCair.Zen. 145.16 (iii B.C.), cf. PSI 4.438.10 - 13 (iii B.C.). flocks and herds, cattle, ἀπογραφὴ λείας PHib. 1.33.2 (iii B.C.), cf. PPetr. 3p.279 (iii B.C.), BGU 1012 (ii B.C.), D.S. 19.21 , 97 ; ἀτέλεια τῆς λ. OGI 748.9 (Cyzic., iii B.C.). (Lit. the people's property, cf. Lat. populari 'plunder'.)
greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ πέμπτον ἔξωθεν μὲν ἐπιφανείᾳ λείᾳ περιγράφεται, τὴν δ’ ἐντὸς οὐσίαν ἔχει τραχεῖαν, οὐδεμίαν μὲν ἔχον ὀσμὴν, ἐν τῇ γεύσει δὲ δριμὺ φαινόμενον· ἔστι γὰρ δήπου καὶ θερμότατον ἁπάντων τῶν ἀλκυονίων, ὡς τρίχας ἀποκάειν δύνασθαι.
english_sentence_A: The fifth is bounded on the outside by a smooth surface, but has its inner substance rough, having no smell, but appearing pungent to the taste; for it is indeed also the hottest of all the alkyonia, so that it is able to burn off hairs.
english_sentence_B: The fifth is bounded on the outside by a smooth surface but has a rough substance within. It has no smell at all but is perceived as pungent to the taste; for it is, of course, also the hottest of all the alkyonia, so that it can burn off hair.

lsj_entry_text: λειχήν, ῆνος, ὁ, tree-moss, lichen, implied in Thphr. (cf. λειχηνιάω). a kind of liver-wort, that grows on damp rocks, Dsc. 4.53 ; but ἵππειος λ., = ἱππολειχήν , Nic. Th. 945 . a lichen-like eruption on the skin of animals, esp. on the chin, mentagra, A. Ch. 281 (pl.), Hp. Aph. 3.20 (pl.), Thphr. Sud. 14 (pl.), LXX Le. 21.20 , Gal. 14.75 , Aët. 8.16 ; also, of the ground, blight, canker, A. Eu. 785 (lyr.). in horses, the normal callosity on foreleg, chestnut, Dsc. 2.43 (pl.), Cael.Aur. TP 1.138 (pl.).—In codd. freq. written λιχήν.
greek_sentence: διὸ τῶν μὲν πρώτων δύο λειχῆνας καὶ ἀλφοὺς καὶ μέντοι καὶ ψώρας καὶ λέπρας ὠφελούντων, ἔτι τε λαμπρυνόντων τὸ δέρμα διὰ τὸ σύμμετρον τῆς δυνάμεως, δύναται ταὐτὸ ποιεῖν τουτὶ τὸ ἔσχατον εἰρημένον.
english_sentence_A: Therefore, while the first two benefit lichens and alphoi and indeed also psorai and lepra, and further brighten the skin owing to the due measure of their power, this last-mentioned one can do the same thing.
english_sentence_B: Therefore, while the first two benefit leichenes and alphoi, and indeed also psorai and leprai, and moreover make the skin bright because of the moderateness of their power, this last-mentioned one is able to do the same.

lsj_entry_text: λέπρ-α, Ion. λέπρ-ρη, ἡ, (λεπίς) leprosy, which makes the skin scaly, Hdt. 1.138 , Hp. Aph. 3.20 (pl.), Prorrh. 2.43 (pl.), Epid. 5.9 (sg.), Morb. 1.3 (sg.), Arist. Pr. 887a34 , Thphr. Char. 19.2 , Sud. 14 , LXX Le. 13.2 .

english_sentence_A: Therefore, while the first two benefit lichens and alphoi and indeed also psorai and lepra, and further brighten the skin owing to the due measure of their power, this last-mentioned one can do the same thing.
english_sentence_B: Therefore, while the first two benefit leichenes and alphoi, and indeed also psorai and leprai, and moreover make the skin bright because of the moderateness of their power, this last-mentioned one is able to do the same.

lsj_entry_text: ὀρυκ-τός, ή, όν, dug, formed by digging, τάφρον ὑπερθορέονται ὀρυκτήν Il. 8.179 , al., cf. X. An. 1.7.14 ; opp. a natural channel, στόματα, opp.ἰθαγενέα, Hdt. 2.17 ; λίμνη ib. 149 ; τάφος E. Tr. 1153 ; εἴσοδοι X. An. 4.5.25 ; ἀποθῆκαι ὀ. ὑπόγειοι Plu. 2.770e . dug out, quarried, of stone or metal, τὰ ὀ., opp. τὰ μεταλλευτά, Arist. Mete. 378a20 ; ὀ. χρυσός Plb. 34.10.10 ; ἅλες Gal. 11.694 ; ἅλς Dsc. 5.109 ; ἰχθῦς ὀ. fish taken by digging in sand, such as sand-eels, Arist. Mir. 835b16 , Thphr. Fr. 171.7 , cf. Ath. 8.331c , Archestr. Fr. 22 .
greek_sentence: Περὶ ἁλῶν.] Ἅλες τῆς αὐτῆς κατὰ γένος δυνάμεως οἴ τ’ ὀρυκτοὶ καὶ οἱ θαλάττιοι.
english_sentence_A: On salts.] Salts, both the mined and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind.
english_sentence_B: On salts.] Salts, both the dug and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind.

lsj_entry_text: θαλάσσ-ιος, later Att. θαλάσσ-ττιος, α, ον, also ος, ον E. IT 236 : (θάλασσα):— of, in, on, or from the sea, οὔ σφι θ. ἔργα μεμήγει Il. 2.614 ; κορῶναι εἰνάλιαι, τῇσίν τε θ. ἔργα μέμηλεν Od. 5.67 ; θ. βίος Archil. 51 ; χέλυς Alc. 51 ; θ. ἀνέμων ῥιπαί, κλύδων, Pi. lsj_entry_text: στύφ-ω, Hp. Int. 14 , etc.: aor. inf. στύψαι Hsch. :— Pass. (v.infr.):—contract, draw together, τὴν κοιλίην στύφεσθαι becomes costive, Hp. Aër. 7 ; στῦψαι πλάδον Aret. CA 1.1 ; esp. of an astringent taste, χείλεα στυφθείς having his lips drawn up by the taste, AP 9.375 ; δέρμα ἐστυμμένον, i.e. made watertight, Gal. 12.846 ; mix with στυπτηρία, PMag.Leid.V. 6.18 ; aor. 2 part. Pass. στυφέντα in this last sense, PHolm. 24.13 (στυφόεντα cj. Lagercrantz): metaph. of sounds, φωναὶ στύφουσαι τὴν ἀκοήν, opp. διαχέουσαι, D.H. Comp. 15 . in dyeing, treat fabrics, etc., with a mordant, Lysis ap. Iamb. VP 17.76 ; στῦψον τῇ ἰσάτι prepare it by a preliminary dyeing with woad, PHolm. 21.42 ; στύφει [τὴν ἄγχουσαν] fixes alkanet, ib. 15.18 . intr. in Act. , στύφει κατ' ὀλίγον τὸ οὖρον gradually diminishes, Hp. Int. 14 . intr., to be astringent, Arist. Pr. 863b17 , Philonid. ap. Ath. 15.675e , Dsc. 1.116 , 118 , Sor. 1.81 , Gal. 6.68 , Hices. ap. Ath. 7.321a . metaph., to be harsh, austere, gloomy, Them. Or. 27.339a , cf. Hsch. s.v. στύψαι. [υ , Nic. Al. 278 , cf. 375 (ἐν-); υ to be assumed in στυφέντα (s.v.l.).]
greek_sentence: διαφέρουσι δὲ τῷ μᾶλλον πεπιλῆσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν τῶν ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἁλῶν, διὸ καὶ τὸ παχυμερές τε καὶ στῦφον ἐν τούτοις μᾶλλόν ἐστιν.
english_sentence_A: They differ, however, in that the substance of the salts from the earth is more compacted, for which reason the coarse-particled and astringent element is greater in these.
english_sentence_B: They differ in that the substance of the salts from the earth is more compacted, which is why the coarse-particled and the astringent are present to a greater degree in these.

lsj_entry_text: ποιότης, ητος, ἡ, quality, Pl. Tht. 182a (where he apologizes for the use of the word as ἀλλόκοτον ὄνομα), Arist. Cat. 8b26 , EN 1173a15 (pl.), Gal. Nat.Fac. 1.2 , POxy. 2113.16 (iv A.D.), etc.; of size, Babr. 28.10 , Aesop. 84 .
greek_sentence: λέλεκται δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν Σοδομηνῶν τῶν ἐν τῇ νεκρᾷ θαλάσσῃ καλουμένῃ γεννωμένων ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ γράμματι, καὶ εἴ τις ἐκεῖνο τὸ βιβλίον ἀνέγνωκεν ἐπιμελῶς, ἀναμνήσεως αὐτῷ μόνον δεήσει νῦν, ὥστε ῥηθείσης τῆς γευστῆς ποιότητος αὐτὸν ἐπίστασθαι τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ φαρμάκου.
english_sentence_A: Something has also been said in the fourth book about the Sodomene salts, those produced in the so-called Dead Sea, and if anyone has read that book carefully, he will now need only a reminder, so that, once the gustatory quality has been stated, he may know the power of the drug.
english_sentence_B: The Sodomene salts, produced in what is called the Dead Sea, have also been discussed in the fourth book, and if anyone has read that book carefully, he will now need only to be reminded, so that, once the quality perceived by taste has been stated, he will know the power of the drug.

lsj_entry_text: ἁλυκ-ός, ή, όν, salt, Hp. Acut. 42 , Aër. 1 , Ar. Lys. 403 , LXX Ge. 14.3 ; brackish, Thphr. HP 4.3.5 .
greek_sentence: τῆς οὖν ἁλυκῆς ποιότητος διαφορούσης τε ἅμα καὶ συναγούσης τὴν πλησιάζουσαν οὐσίαν, τὸ καλούμενον ἀφρόνιτρον ἐν τούτῳ τὴν διαφορὰν ἔχει, καθόσον ἕνα μόνον ἐν τούτῳ τὸν ἐπικρατοῦντα χυμὸν ἐναργῶς ἔστιν ἰδεῖν, ὃν ὀνομάζουσι πικρὸν, διαφορητικὴν ἔχοντα δύναμιν, συνακτικὴν δ’ οὐκ ἔχοντα, καθάπερ οἱ ἅλες.
english_sentence_A: Since, then, the salty quality at once disperses and draws together the substance that comes near it, the so-called aphronitron has its difference in this, insofar as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, which has a dispersing power but does not have a contracting one, as salts do.
english_sentence_B: Since, then, the salty quality both disperses and at the same time draws together the substance it comes near, what is called aphronitron differs in this respect, inasmuch as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, having a dispersing power but not having a drawing-together power, as salts do.

lsj_entry_text: ἀφρόνιτρον, Att. ἀφρόλιτρον (the two distd. by Gal.l.c., cf. Gp. 2.28 ), τό, a form of native sodium carbonate (cf.νίτρον), distd. by Gal. 12.212 from the finer ἄνθος νίτρου, cf. Herod.Med. ap. Orib. 6.20.5 : in Hp. and correct Greek divisim ἀφρὸς νίτρου: hence ἀφρόνιτρον is condemned by Phryn. 272 .

english_sentence_B: Since, then, the salty quality both disperses and at the same time draws together the substance it comes near, what is called aphronitron differs in this respect, inasmuch as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, having a dispersing power but not having a drawing-together power, as salts do.

lsj_entry_text: περισσ-ωματικός, Att. περιττ-, ή, όν, of the nature of περιττώματα, excretive, excrementitious, ἀπόκρισις Arist. PA 681b36 ; ὑγρότης Plu. 2.130b ; π. [μόριον] for excretion, Arist. HA 531a29 , etc. of persons, abounding in περιττώματα, ib. 584a6 , Pr. 873a18 ; σώματα Id. GA 766b35 ( Comp. ); βρέφη Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.2 ; π. καὶ παχὺς τὴν σάρκα, of a pig, Jul. Or. 5.177c .
greek_sentence: οὗτοι γὰρ ὅσον μὲν ὑγρόν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς σώμασι, τοῦτο πᾶν ἐκβόσκονται· τὸ δ’ ὑπόλοιπον τῆς στερεᾶς οὐσίας συνάγουσι τῇ στύψει, διὸ καὶ ταριχεύουσι καὶ ἄσηπτα φυλάσσουσι τὰ σώματα τῶν σηπομένων, ὑγρότητα περιττωματικὴν ἐχόντων ἀδιάλυτόν τε καὶ ἄσφιγκτον τὴν οὐσίαν.
english_sentence_A: For salts consume all that is moist in bodies; and the remainder of the solid substance they draw together by their astringency, for which reason they also pickle, and keep free of putrefaction, the bodies of things that putrefy, which have a superfluous moisture and a substance that is loose (ἀδιάλυτον) and not compacted.
english_sentence_B: For salts consume all the moisture that is in bodies, while the remainder of the solid substance they draw together by their astringency; for this reason they also pickle, and keep unputrefied, the bodies of things that putrefy, which have residual moisture that is undissipated and a substance that is not tightly bound.

lsj_entry_text: περισσός, Att. περιττός, ή, όν, (from περί, as ἔπισσαι from ἐπί, μέτασσαι from μετά) beyond the regular number or size, prodigious, δῶρα Hes. Th. 399 (never in Hom. ); ῶʼμος Trag.Adesp. 458.3 ; στάθμα, dub.sens., v. ἕλκω B. 3 . out of the common, extraordinary, strange, ἔ τι περισσὸν εἰδείη if he has any signal knowledge, Thgn. 769 ; εἴ τι φρονεῖς καί τι περισσὸν ἔχεις Philisc.( PLG 2.327 ); π. λόγος S. OT 841 ; ἄγρα E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); πάθος Id. Supp. 791 (lyr.); βίος οὐδὲν ἔχων π. ἀλλὰ πάντα σμικρά Antipho Soph. 51 ; οὐ γὰρ π. οὐδὲν οὐδ' ἔξω λόγου πέπονθας E. Hipp. 437 ; περισσότερα παθήματα Antipho 3.4.5 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἔργων καὶ τερατώδη Isoc. 12.77 ; ἴδια καὶ π. Id. 15.145 ; π. καὶ θαυμαστά Arist. EN 1141b6 ; πρᾶξις π. Id. Pol. 1312a27 ; οὐθὲν δὴ λέγοντες π. φαίνονταί τι λέγειν Id. Metaph. 1053b3 ; τί π. ποιεῖτε; Ev.Matt. 5.47 ; περιττοτάτη φύσις Arist. HA 531a9 ; συνανθρωπίζον . . πάντων περισσότατον, of the dog, Ath. 13.611c , cf. Clearch. 24 ; in Literature, striking, τὸ περιττόν, as a quality of οἱ τοῦ Σωκράτους λόγοι, Arist. Pol. 1265a11 ; τὰ σοφὰ καὶ τὰ π. refinements, Epicur. Fr. 409 ; opp. κοινὸς καὶ δημώδης, Longin. 40.2 (but also, elaborate, π. καὶ πεποιημένος Id. 3.4 ; in bad sense, far-fetched, D.H. Pomp. 2 , Dem. 56 ). of persons, extraordinary, remarkable, esp. for great learning, π. ὢν ἀνήρ E. Hipp. 948 ; τοὺς . . π. καί τι πράσσοντας πλέον Id. Fr. 788 ; δυστυχεῖς εἶναι τοὺς π. Arist. Metaph. 983a2 ; π. γένος τῶν μελιττῶν Id. GA 760a4 : freq. with the manner added, π. κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν Id. Pr. 953a10 ; περὶ τὸν ἄλλον βίον περιττότερος somewhat extravagant or eccentric, Id. Pol. 1267 b24 ; τῇ φύσει π. Id. HA 622b6 ; κάλλει Plu. Demetr. 2 ; ἐν ἅπασι Id. Dem. 3 ; τὴν ὥραν Alciphr. 1.12 : c. inf., D.H. Comp. 18 . c. gen., περισσὸς ἄλλων πρός τι beyond others in . . , S. El. 155 ; θύσει τοῦδε περισσότερα greater things than this, AP 6.321 (Leon. Alex. ); περιττότερος προφήτου one greater than . . , Ev.Matt. 11.9 . more than sufficient, superfluous, αἱ π. δαπάναι X. Mem. 3.6.6 ; περιττὸν ἔχειν to have a surplus, Id. An. 7.6.31 ; οἱ μὲν . . περιττὰ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα . . Id. Oec. 20.1 : c. gen., τῶν ἀρκούντων περιττά more than sufficient, Id. Cyr. 8.2.21 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἱκανῶν Id. Hier. 1.19 : freq. in military sense, οἱ π. ἱππεῖς the reserve horse, Id. Eq.Mag. 8.14 ; οἱ π. τῆς φυλακῆς ib. 7.7 ; π. σκηναί spare tents, Id. Cyr. 4.6.12 (but τοῖς περιττοῖς χρήσεσθαι their superior numbers, Id. An. 4.8.11 , cf. Cyr. 6.3.20 ); τὸ π. the surplus, residue, Inscr. ap. eund. An. 5.3.13 (but τὸ π. τοῦ Ἰουδαίου the advantage of the Jew, Ep.Rom. 3.1 ); Ἁρπυιῶν τὰ π. their leavings, AP 11.239 ( Lucill. ); τὸ π. τῆς ἡμέρας the remainder of the day, X.Eph. 1.3 ; π. γράμματα supplementary provisions in a will, BGU 326ii9 (ii A.D.). in bad sense, superfluous, useless, οὐδέ τι τοῦ παντὸς κενεὸν πέλει οὐδὲ π. Emp. 13 ; μόχθος π. A. Pr. 385 , cf. S. Ant. 780 ; π. κἀνόνητα σώματα Id. Aj. 758 ; βάρος π. γῆς ἀναστρωφώμενοι Id. Fr. 945 ; ἄχθος Id. El. 1241 (lyr.); τὰ γὰρ π. πανταχοῦ λυπήρ' ἔπη Id. Fr. 82 ; αὐδῶ σε μὴ περισσὰ κηρύσσειν A. Th. 1048 ; π. πάντες οὑν μέσῳ λόγοι E. Med. 819 ; π. φωνῶν Id. Supp. 459 . excessive, extravagant, μηχανᾶσθαι περισσά commit extravagances, Hdt. 2.32 ; περισσὰ δρᾶν, πράσσειν, to be over-busy, S. Tr. 617 , Ant. 68 ; π. φρονεῖν to be over-wise, E. Fr. 924 (anap.); ἡ π. αὕτη ἐπιμέλεια τοῦ σώματος Pl. R. 407b ; μῆκος πολὺ λόγων π. Id. Lg. 645c ; redundant, overdone, οἱ καρτεροὶ καὶ π. λόγοι Id. Ax. 365c , etc.; of dress, ἐσθὴς π. Hipp. 445 , cf. Ba. 429 (lyr.); ὁ πολυπράγμων καὶ π. Plb. 9.1.4 ; τὴν περὶ τὸ σῶμα θεραπείαν ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. Plu. english_sentence_A: Accordingly, bodies in which there is no superfluous moisture at all, as in the finest honey, and whose solid body is compacted, as in stones, cannot putrefy; wherefore the use of salts is not well regarded in the case of these, but in those cases where putrefaction is suspected.

greek_sentence: Περὶ ἁλῶν κεκαυμένων.] Ἅλες κεκαυμένοι τὸ μὲν διαφορητικὸν μᾶλλον ἔχουσι τῶν ἀκαύστων, εἰς ὅσον αὐτῶν λεπτομερέστερον γίγνεται τὸ σῶμα, τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς λαμβάνον δύναμιν, ὡς κᾀπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐδείχθη τῶν κεκαυμένων συμβαίνειν, οὐ μὴν ὁμοίως γε τοῖς ἀκαύστοις συνάγειν καὶ πιλοῦν τὴν στερεὰν οὐσίαν ἔτι δύνανται.
english_sentence_A: On burnt salt.] Burnt salt has the dispersing property more than unburnt salt, to the extent that its body becomes more fine-particled, taking on its power from the fire, as was shown to happen in the case of the other burnt substances too; yet it is no longer able, in the same way as unburnt salt, to draw together and compact the solid substance.
english_sentence_B: On burnt salt.] Burnt salt has the dispersing [property] to a greater degree than unburnt salt, in proportion as its body becomes more fine-particled, taking on a power from the fire, as was shown to happen also in the case of the other burnt [substances]; it is not, however, still able to draw together and compact the solid substance in the same way as unburnt salt.

english_sentence_A: The power of the drug is drying and heating, in roughly the second order.
english_sentence_B: The power of the drug is drying and heating, somewhere about the second order.

lsj_entry_text: ἔναιμ-ος, ον, with blood in one, θεοὶ ἔ. καὶ σαρκώδεις of flesh and blood, Hdt. 3.29 ; charged with blood, opp. ἄναιμος, ἔναιμον καὶ πυκνόν, οἷον ἧπαρ Hp. VM 22 ; πλεύμων Arist. HA 489a30 , PA 690b11 , al. Χρῶμα ἔ. blood-colour, Pl. Ti. 68b . metaph., full of blood, vigorous, Χλωρὰ καὶ ἔ. τὰ πράγματα Gorg. ap. Arist. Rh. 1406b9 (nisi leg. ἄναιμα). ἔναιμα (sc. φάρμακα) medicaments for stanching blood, Hp. Art. 63 : sg., Fract. 24 ; φάρμακον ἔ. Thphr. HP 4.7.2 . ἔ. ἀγωγή treatment of bleeding wounds, Orib. 46.8.15 , cf. 45.18.31 . Adv. -μως ibid., Antyll.ib. 44.23.46 .

english_sentence_A: Reasonably, then, they use it for the agglutination of bloody wounds, and for the other conditions, all those that require to be dried together with a moderate heating.
english_sentence_B: Reasonably, then, it is used for the agglutination of fresh bleeding wounds, [and] for the other things that need drying together with moderate heating.

lsj_entry_text: αἱμο-ρραγία, ἡ, haemorrhage, Hp. Art. 69 , Aph. 7.21 ; any violent bleeding, ib. 5.16 ; nose-bleeding, Gal. 17(1).50 , etc.
greek_sentence: ἐχρῆτο δ’ αὐτῷ τις τῶν ἡμετέρων διδασκάλων καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐν ταῖς χειρουργίαις αἱμοῤῥαγίας, ἕτοιμον ἔχων ξηρὸν μὲν καὶ ἄνικμον, δεδευμένον δὲ μάλιστα μὲν ἀσφάλτῳ, μὴ παρούσης δὲ ταύτης πίττῃ, προσετίθει δ’ αὐτὸν τοῖς αἱμοῤῥαγοῦσι χωρίοις, ἔτι καιόμενον, ὡς ἐσχαροῦσθαί τε ἅμα τὸ μόριον καὶ οἷον πῶμά τι λαμβάνειν αὐτὸ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ καυθέντος σπόγγου.
english_sentence_A: One of our teachers used it also for the haemorrhages that occur in surgical operations, keeping it ready, dry and devoid of moisture, soaked preferably in asphalt, or, if this was not at hand, in pitch; and he applied it to the bleeding places while it was still burning, so that the part was at once made to form an eschar and the body of the burnt sponge itself was received as a kind of stopper.
english_sentence_B: He kept it ready, dry and without moisture, but soaked, preferably in asphalt, or in pitch if asphalt was not available. He applied it, still burning, to the haemorrhaging places, so that the part was at the same moment turned into an eschar and received the very body of the burnt sponge as a kind of lid.

english_sentence_A: You will know this if you use it on a wound by itself with water or oxykraton (vinegar-and-water) or wine, according to the differences of bodies, as has been said before; for it will glue them together much like the drugs called enaima (those for bloody wounds).
english_sentence_B: You will know this if you use it on its own on a wound, with water or oxycrate or wine according to the differences of the bodies, as was said before. For it will agglutinate them in a way similar to the drugs called enhaemous.
